slides.headline: SOUND SENIOR BEFORE YOU ARE
slides.body: Five habits you can practise before your next interview.
Two candidates give the same answer. The calm one is the one the panel pictures in the job.

slides.headline: SETTLE BEFORE YOU SPEAK
slides.body: On a call, camera on and framed before they join. In a room, stand, eye contact, then your name. Two still seconds.

slides.headline: LET THE SILENCE SIT
slides.body: Finish your answer, then stop. No "so yeah", no second version. Count two in your head and let them speak.

slides.headline: PICK A SIDE OUT LOUD
slides.body: Asked which option you'd choose? "I'd pick B, because it ships sooner." A clear call beats a tour of both.

slides.headline: SLOW DOWN ON HARD QUESTIONS
slides.body: "Tell me about a time you failed." Breathe once, then answer at your normal pace. Rushing is what reads as nerves.

slides.headline: CLOSE WITH ONE CLEAR LINE
slides.body: For example: "I want this role, and I'd start with your onboarding backlog." Then thank them and stop.

slides.headline: SAVE THIS
slides.body: Run through it on the way to your next panel round.

caption:
Two candidates give the same answer. Only one of them sounds ready to lead.

The gap usually isn't the words. It's what happens around them: the 2 seconds before you start on Zoom, the pause after you finish, how you take the hard question from the VP on the panel.

That's executive presence. People talk about it like a personality trait. It works more like 5 habits, and you can rehearse every one.

Pick 1 per mock interview, Monday to Friday. Settle first. Let silence sit. Pick a side. Slow down when it's hard. Close with 1 line.

Most interview tips are about what to say. These are about how you hold the room while you say it.

Save this for the night before your panel round.
